In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1].

mitigation_mechanism: Studies disagree on whether agroforestry reduces drought losses, and the split runs between sub-practices. On the benefit side: in Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, farmers said deep-rooted trees reach water from deep down and keep producing fruit when there is no rain, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind; the study concludes that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought, citing deep root systems that use a greater soil volume for water [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10, ev_t3_drought_roots_quandt17_2, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. Trees also share deep water and act as a fodder reserve: hydraulic redistribution in Sahelian parklands lets crop roots use deep soil moisture reached only by tree roots, millet with the shrub Guiera senegalensis in the Sahel produced over 900% more biomass under water stress, and trees were the main source of feed and milk for Zambian agro-pastoralists during drought [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3, ev_crop_yield_santos25_1, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14]. In an induced drought in eastern Canada only the monocrop lost yield, agroforestry biomass in the Brazilian semi-arid varied far less over 4 years than conventional systems, and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Nyando District, Kenya, households in an agroforestry project typically used fewer detrimental coping strategies during hunger periods, and many farmers reported selling fuel wood and timber from their trees to buy food during the drought [ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In Sahelian parklands, trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25% [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. Live fences of species such as Gliricidia sepium and Leucaena leucocephala supply livestock fodder in the dry season, when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]. For shaded coffee and cocoa: in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest, the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly raised coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; and reviews cite a 41% cut in evapotranspiration loss under coffee shade trees in the hot, dry season and low water stress in cacao grown with Gliricidia [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11].
caveats: The roll-up is conflicting because the sub-practice cells disagree: the regeneration-on-farmland, planted silvoarable and silvopastoral cells read as benefits, while the linear-boundary and shaded perennial-crop cells are themselves conflicting. The clearest harm finding is a direct field measurement in Ghana: during the extreme drought of 2015/16 all cocoa plants under Albizia ferruginea shade trees died and cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality, while cocoa in full sun kept higher sap flux and soil water content was higher in full sun, pointing to competition for water between shade trees and cocoa [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. What separates the sides is mainly system and severity: deep-rooted trees in dryland fields and fodder trees in pastures read as buffers, while in shaded tree crops under extreme drought the trees compete with the crop for scarce soil water. Trade-offs pull the other way: tree–maize competition for soil water in Kenya can lead to crop failure, and a Senegal review finds no clear consensus on windbreak hedges in drought, with some studies reporting higher yields in drier years and others harm to rainfed crops [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10, ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17]. The understorey yield benefit holds in drought years only, since tree shade can lower understorey yields under normal rainfall, and the Kenyan household link to perceived drought held in Burat but not in Kinna [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5]. Several units are proxies or ratings rather than measurements: the Canadian and US units are high-income evidence, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_t3_water_infiltration_batcheler24_9, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. A cited temperate finding of greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years adds to the counter-evidence, the German soil-water difference was not significant everywhere and is high-income evidence, and the Nyando timber-sales finding is farmer-reported [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the Quesungual system, so it may overstate the benefit; it does not say how severe the 1997 dry period was, and the trees come bundled with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. The parkland fodder statement is a review citation without a size [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. The Latin American silvopastoral units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year rather than with and without trees, and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. The Ethiopian Faidherbia result is a drought-year comparison reported as an 'up to' figure; the same study reports its normal-season gain separately, so this hazard-year gain is not the usual yield effect [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. In shaded cocoa and coffee the evidence is split: reviews cite that under warmer, water-limited conditions competition between trees and cacao for scarce soil water can reduce soil moisture and cacao yields below those of open-sun farms, and that intercropping may compete for soil moisture during drought [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_soil_water_retention_patil25_8]; and in the Ghana experiment the shade-by-drought interaction on yield was not significant, so shade did not prevent the drought-induced yield decline and only partly compensated for it [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]; the Ethiopian study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in the extreme climate shocks [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]; and across cabruca cocoa farms in southern Bahia, Brazil, drought yield loss was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2].
caveats: Apart from the Ethiopian paired-plot study, which is a drought-year result reported as an 'up to' figure with its normal-season gain reported separately [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2], the literature units are reviews citing earlier work, and the deep-water unit enters as a component of drought impact rather than a measured drought loss [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3]. The FMNR unit is a compiler rating of a slight benefit on a technology sheet, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The parkland fodder statement is a review citation without a size [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the Quesungual system, so it may overstate the benefit; it does not say how severe the 1997 dry period was, and the trees come bundled with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2].

On the competing side, the strongest measurement is a Ghana field study of a cocoa plantation through the extreme 2015/16 El Niño drought: all cocoa plants under the shade tree Albizia ferruginea died, cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality with sap flux density cut to 115 g cm2 day1 against 170 in full sun, sap-flux recovery afterwards was 163 in full sun against 37 under Antiaris, and soil water was higher in full sun, which the authors link to strong competition for soil water [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. Reviews add that under warmer, water-limited conditions tree-cacao competition can push soil moisture and cacao yields below open-sun farms (Blaser et al. 2018), and that intercropping may compete for soil moisture during drought [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_soil_water_retention_patil25_8]. mitigation_mechanism: Trees were the most important source of animal feed and milk for Zambian agro-pastoralists during drought, and agroforestry in Brazil's semi-arid region had much less year-to-year variation in biomass productivity than conventional systems, attributed mainly to water availability [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25% [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2].

mitigation_mechanism: On rainfed cropland the evidence divides on whether trees add water the crop can use or compete with the crop for it. Hydraulic redistribution in Sahelian parklands lets crop roots use deep soil moisture reached only by tree roots, and in the Sahel millet intercropped with the shrub Guiera senegalensis produced over 900% more biomass under water stress [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3, ev_crop_yield_santos25_1]. In an experimentally induced drought in eastern Canada, crop losses occurred in the monocrop only, not in the soybean intercropping agroforestry system, and during drought understorey crop yield can be higher than in an open system even under intense shade [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]; the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In a German alley-cropping system during a drought year, soil water content stayed lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though the differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns gave up to 85% more grain than open-field wheat in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low [ev_crop_yield_sida18_2].
caveats: The sub-practices disagree, so the roll-up states conflicting evidence. On the gain side, regeneration-based farmland holds the stronger result and reads as a benefit throughout: Sahelian parkland trees make deep soil moisture available to crop roots, the FMNR compiler rates drought impacts as mitigated, Quesungual farmers reported no total maize loss in the 1997 El Niño dry period, and Ethiopian wheat under Faidherbia albida out-yielded open-field wheat in the El Niño year, a hazard-year result kept apart from the study's normal-season gain [ev_soil_water_retention_vannoordwijk21_3, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2]. On the conflicting side, planted silvoarable systems pair gains (the Canadian induced drought, the Sahelian millet–Guiera result, German alley-cropping soil water) with a reversal, Kenyan maize under Grevillea robusta, where competition for limited soil water delayed flowering and can lead to crop failure [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_crop_yield_santos25_1, ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_crop_yield_watts22_10]; and boundary plantings pair a live-fence fodder role in drought with greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years and a Senegal review that finds no consensus on windbreak hedges in drought [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3, ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17]. What separates the sides in the units' own words is whether tree roots reach moisture the crop cannot, or compete with the crop for limited soil water close to the trees. The understorey drought-year result sits outside the voting sub-practices, and that benefit reverses under normal rainfall [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. The Canadian result is high-income temperate evidence, the live-fence fodder unit is a pantropical review, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating rather than a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The German soil-water difference was not significant at all positions and is high-income evidence [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the Quesungual system, so it may overstate the benefit; it does not say how severe the 1997 dry period was, and the trees come bundled with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2].

mitigation_mechanism: Households in Isiolo County, Kenya, describe trees that keep producing through drought: one farmer said they planted trees because "they do not dry up fast during times of drought" and still produce fruit with a little watering, and another said of mango trees that their roots travel far and get water from deep down, with mango, papaya and banana listed as the most important species during drought [ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7]. The study's background, citing earlier reviews, names deep root systems that use a greater soil volume for water and nutrients as one reason agroforestry species are resilient to droughts [ev_t3_drought_roots_quandt17_2, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. In both study communities 74% of respondents said they had planted trees with drought in mind, respondents listed agroforestry as important for household livelihood during drought, and in Burat households practising agroforestry largely said droughts were less frequent (64 respondents) while most households without it (46 respondents) said the opposite [ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5]. The authors conclude that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought [ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10].
caveats: Every unit comes from one Kenyan study in semi-arid, lower-middle-income Isiolo County, inside the LIC/LMIC target, so there is no independent second source [ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10]. The units are farmer statements, survey proportions and perceptions rather than measured drought losses, so nothing in this cell puts a size on the effect [ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8]. The perception finding held in Burat only; in Kinna responses did not vary between households with and without agroforestry, and a perception that droughts are less frequent is not a measure of drought impact [ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5]. The deep-root and resilience statements in the introduction repeat earlier work (Kandji et al., Verchot et al. and others), not the study's own result [ev_t3_drought_roots_quandt17_2, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. The trees named are fruit trees on mixed crop-livestock farms; the quotes speak of agroforestry in general rather than a planted silvoarable layout [ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10].

mitigation_mechanism: Under drought, trees in tree-crop systems have been found to protect the crop, to compete with it for water, and to make no difference. On the protective side, in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly raised coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; reviews cite a 41% cut in evapotranspiration loss under coffee shade trees in the hot, dry season (Lin) and low water stress in cacao grown with Gliricidia [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11]; and a review adds that under normal rainfall tree shade can lower understorey crop yields while during drought those yields can be higher than in an open system, even in intense shade [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. General agroforestry reports point the same way: live fences supply livestock fodder in the dry season, when pasture is scarce [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1]; and the Kenyan compiler for Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR) judges that it improves micro-climate and soil moisture and so mitigates drought impacts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. On the competing side, reviews cite that under warmer, water-limited conditions competition between trees and cacao for scarce soil water can reduce soil moisture and cacao yields below those of open-sun farms (Blaser et al.), and that intercropping may compete for soil moisture during drought [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_soil_water_retention_patil25_8]; the field study by Abdulai et al. in Ghana measured this directly: during the extreme drought of 2015/16 all cocoa plants under Albizia ferruginea shade trees died, cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality with sap flux density cut to 115 against 170 in full sun (grams per square centimetre per day), sap flux recovered to 163 in full sun but only 37 under A. toxicaria, and soil water was higher in full sun, which the authors link to strong competition for soil water [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]; earlier work (Kowalchuk and Jong) cited in a German alley-cropping study found greater crop yield losses near shelterbelts in dry years because of competition [ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3]. Between them sit no-effect findings: in a Ghanaian throughfall-exclusion experiment the shade-by-drought interaction on cocoa yield was not significant, so shade may not prevent the yield decline under drought [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]; the Ethiopian coffee study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in extreme climate shocks [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]; and on Bahia cocoa farms drought yield loss was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2].
caveats: The studies disagree, so the row states no direction. What separates the sides, as far as the evidence says, is whether the trees draw on the same scarce soil water as the crop: the losses are attributed to that competition, measured in the Ghanaian shade-tree study (Abdulai et al.) as lower soil water under the shade trees than in full sun, while the gains come with a named companion tree (Gliricidia), a shade-management setting (canopy openness) or a drought year in which shade relieved the understorey [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1, ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13]. A second separator is what is measured: the Ghanaian throughfall-exclusion experiment found the overall better performance of cocoa under shade can only partly compensate for the reduced yield during drought, so a higher yield under shade is not the same as protection from drought [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. Shade-tree species is a third: in the Abdulai study every cocoa plant under Albizia ferruginea died against 77% under Antiaris toxicaria [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. Tree species, density and canopy management are therefore the design questions for drought-exposed tree-crop systems. The cocoa and coffee units are crop-specific and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; the throughfall-exclusion experiment's shade came from artificial shade nets rather than shade trees, so its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. Many units on both sides are second-hand readings in reviews [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_patil25_8, ev_crop_yield_watts22_8]; the Abdulai shade-tree study, measured on a single farm, is the field anchor of the harm side [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. Only the cocoa and coffee units record a tree-perennial system; the live-fence, FMNR, understorey and shelterbelt units record none and are applied here by default, and the FMNR unit is a compiler rating rather than a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_crop_yield_majaura25_3]. The field units are from low-income Ethiopia, lower-middle-income Ghana and upper-middle-income Brazil [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1, ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2].

On the harm side, a field study in Ghana found that during the extreme drought of 2015/16 all cocoa plants under Albizia ferruginea shade trees died and cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality, while cocoa in full sun kept higher sap flux; soil water content was higher in full sun, which the authors link to stronger competition for water in the shaded systems [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1].

mitigation_mechanism: Under drought, shade over cocoa and coffee has been found to protect the crop, to compete with it for water, and to make no difference. On the protective side, in Ethiopia's Yayu coffee forest the yield model for the climate-shock years found leguminous shade strongly raised coffee shrub yields at high canopy openness [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]; a review cites a 41% cut in evapotranspiration loss under coffee shade trees in the hot, dry season (Lin 2006) [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8]; and another cites low water stress in cacao grown with Gliricidia (Schwendenmann et al. 2010; Köhler et al. 2010) [ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11]. On the competing side, the strongest measurement is a Ghana field study of a cocoa plantation through the extreme 2015/16 El Niño drought: all cocoa plants under the shade tree Albizia ferruginea died, cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality with sap flux density cut to 115 g cm2 day1 against 170 in full sun, sap-flux recovery afterwards was 163 in full sun against 37 under Antiaris, and soil water was higher in full sun, which the authors link to strong competition for soil water [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. Reviews add that under warmer, water-limited conditions tree-cacao competition can push soil moisture and cacao yields below open-sun farms (Blaser et al. 2018), and that intercropping may compete for soil moisture during drought [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_soil_water_retention_patil25_8]. Between them sit no-effect findings: in a Ghana rainwater-suppression experiment the shade-by-drought interaction on yield was not significant, so shade did not prevent the drought-induced yield decline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]; the Ethiopian study did not directly observe benefits of diverse shade in the extreme climate shock [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]; and across cabruca cocoa farms in southern Bahia, Brazil, drought yield loss was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2].
caveats: Studies disagree, and what separates the sides, as far as the evidence says, is twofold. First, whether the shade trees draw on the same scarce soil water as the crop: the losses, including the Ghana die-off, are attributed to that competition [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1, ev_crop_yield_watts22_8], while the gains come with a named companion tree (Gliricidia) or a shade-management setting (canopy openness) [ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1]. Shade-tree species, density and canopy management are therefore the design questions; in the Ghana study the outcome differed by shade-tree species, total loss under one and heavy loss under the other [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. Second, a higher yield under shade is not the same as protection from drought: the Ghana experiment found the better performance of cocoa under shade can only partly compensate for the reduced yield during drought episodes [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. The Ghana experiment's shade came from artificial shade nets, not shade trees, so it has no below-ground competition and its transfer to agroforestry is borderline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]. All units are crop-specific (cocoa or coffee) and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop. The Ghana die-off was measured in an extreme drought; most other units do not say how severe the drought was [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]. The review units are second-hand readings of earlier studies, and only the evapotranspiration figure carries a size [ev_soil_water_retention_dobhal24_8, ev_soil_water_retention_watts22_11, ev_crop_yield_watts22_8, ev_soil_water_retention_patil25_8]. The field units are from upper-middle-income Brazil, low-income Ethiopia and lower-middle-income Ghana; the review units record no country [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1].

mitigation_mechanism: The silvopasture study in this cell compared silvopasture with non-grazed managed forest in Washington State, USA: silvopasture management reduced grass biomass, litter and duff depth, and the authors conclude that managing overstory, understory and grazing together can reduce fuel loads and potential wildfire risk [ev_t3_fuel_load_abstract_batcheler24_1, ev_t3_litter_duff_batcheler24_5]. Rotational grazing removes understory biomass and herbaceous surface fuel, and the reduced, more variable overstory density has the potential to reduce fire frequency compared with other land uses [ev_t3_herbaceous_fuel_batcheler24_4, ev_t3_fire_freq_batcheler24_3]. Rate of fire spread and burn severity correlate with litter and duff depth in this forest type, which is why the litter reduction matters for fire [ev_t3_fire_spread_batcheler24_6]. A land-use overlay of burnt areas across six European Mediterranean countries found that, corrected for the extent of each land use, agroforestry occupied 12% of the area but was associated with only 6% of the fires, while shrubland occupied 16% and was associated with 40%; agroforestry's share was not statistically different from that of forest and grassland [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_1, ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_2]. Before that correction, the average share of fire incidents was lowest for grasslands (11.2%) and agroforestry (20.2%) and highest for shrublands (36.7%) and forests (31.9%) [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_3]. Separately, a Kenyan compiler for farmer managed natural regeneration rates that tree cover can increase the risk of major wild fires, and that fire breaks should be considered for larger sites [ev_fire_hazard_wocat_507_2019_fire_risk].
caveats: None of this evidence can set the class. Every comparison is against the unmanaged state rather than the farming-system counterfactual this cell asks about. The US study compares silvopasture with non-grazed managed forest [ev_t3_fuel_load_abstract_batcheler24_1, ev_t3_litter_duff_batcheler24_5, ev_t3_select_fuels_batcheler24_8], and the Mediterranean overlay compares existing grazed wood-pasture with forest, shrubland and grassland, not with the cropland or open pasture a project would convert [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_1, ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_3]. Against treeless pasture the reading changes: introducing trees adds woody material, litter and duff that open pasture does not have, so having less fuel than a forest does not mean having less fuel than the pasture the practice replaces. Read against that comparator, the fire-spread correlation with litter and duff depth would point to added risk rather than a reduction [ev_t3_fire_spread_batcheler24_6], and in the Mediterranean data grassland, not agroforestry, had the lowest unadjusted share of fires [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_3]. The Mediterranean result that does favour agroforestry is the one against shrubland; against forest and grassland the difference was not significant [ev_fire_hazard_damianidis21_2]. mitigation_mechanism: Measured cooling reaches crops: midday air temperature under Faidherbia albida canopies on Ethiopian wheat farms was up to 6°C lower than in the open field, poplar alley cropping in Germany was 3.4°C cooler than sole wheat on hot days, and lower heat load under Populus deltoides in India raised wheat grain yield by 6.8% [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6]. In the same Ethiopian study, a crop model found that the lower temperature under F. albida shade raised simulated wheat yield when nitrogen was applied, but without applied N simulated yield was extremely small and did not respond to temperature [ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. Silvopastoral systems cut heat stress in cattle: intensive shrub–tree–rotational pasture models in the dry Colombian Caribbean reduce it, and eucalyptus–brachiaria systems in Brazil reduced the area at critical animal thermal-comfort levels by 20 to 100% against monoculture pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. A meta-analysis of field studies on Chinese farmland found summer air temperature 4.01% lower and relative humidity 13.45% higher in shelterbelt-protected than in unsheltered fields [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, maximum daily temperature fell by an average of 1–2.5 °C and minimum air humidity rose by up to 5%, with stronger differences on hotter and drier days [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. Milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover, attributed to less heat stress and more foliage and fruit, and other studies found increases above 15% for cows grazing silvopasture compared with cows in full sun [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2]. Reviews and syntheses report the same cooling more generally: over-storey shade moderates severe temperature (2–4°C) effects on understorey crops, tree shading can lower ambient temperature by 4°C and soil temperature by 6–10°C, agroforestry reduces ambient temperatures and crop heat stress, shade trees buffer rising temperatures to stabilise coffee yields, and shade trees produce microclimates that buffer temperature fluctuations [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_t3_microclimate_shade_quandt17_3]. In Senegal's Ferlo, air temperature under Acacia tortilis ranged between 29 °C and 36 °C against 26 °C to 42 °C outside, and access to the cool zones under trees reduces livestock heat stress and so raises animal productivity [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6, ev_livestock_productivity_faosen24_22]. In cocoa and coffee, a pantropical synthesis found mean temperature lower and daily maximum and minimum temperatures buffered in cocoa agroforestry against monocultures, a review cites shade trees reducing canopy temperatures by 2–4 °C, and measurements in Costa Rican coffee found shade cut maximum air temperature by 1.7 °C [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].
caveats: Cooling under trees is consistent across the units, but most measure temperature or animal comfort rather than a heat-stress loss to crops, herds or income, and none measures the effect in a heat event the authors call severe or extreme, so the class is a slight reduction. Against the cooling, windbreak hedges in Senegal generally cause a slight temperature rise in the protected plots, with effects that vary by crop and growth stage [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. Nearly all units are reviews citing earlier studies. The yield and milk-production units apply to hot conditions only, and the German alley-cropping unit is high-income temperate evidence [ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6, ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4]. Most of the Latin American units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews, while the Brazilian Caatinga preprint measured the thermal indices itself [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]; the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days, and the Costa Rican units are high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. The milk gains mix relief from heat with extra foliage and fruit, so they are not a pure heat-stress effect [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2]. The shelterbelt cooling is a pooled meta-analysis result from upper-middle-income China, expressed as a modest percentage change in air temperature rather than a measured heat-stress loss [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. The Ethiopian cooling was measured on farm, but its yield link is modelled, and the model's null without applied N is among the no-benefit results in this row [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. The IPCC chapter that says shade trees can ameliorate rising stand temperatures for arabica coffee adds in the same sentence that the opposite can also be true [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. The cocoa and coffee units are crop-specific and enter because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop; they report temperature rather than heat-stress losses [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].

A pantropical synthesis of cocoa studies found that the shade-tree canopy reduces solar radiation, so mean temperature stays lower and daily maximum and minimum temperatures are buffered compared with monocultures [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1]. Measured on plots, shade cut maximum air temperature by 1.7 °C in Costa Rican coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].
caveats: The IPCC sentence that credits shade trees adds that the opposite can also be true, so the cooling is not guaranteed [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. All units report temperature, a component of heat-stress impact, not measured crop heat-stress losses, and none is at severe or extreme heat. mitigation_mechanism: Silvopastoral systems cut heat stress in cattle: intensive shrub–tree–rotational pasture models in the dry Colombian Caribbean reduce it, and eucalyptus–brachiaria systems in Brazil reduced the area at critical animal thermal-comfort levels by 20 to 100% against monoculture pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. Tree shade in pastures is associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. Milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover, attributed to less heat stress and more foliage and fruit, and other studies found increases above 15% for cows grazing silvopasture compared with cows in full sun [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2].
caveats: Most units are reviews citing earlier studies, and the shade-associated milk and weight-gain figures are associations rather than measured heat-stress losses avoided [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. Most of the Latin American units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews, while the Brazilian Caatinga preprint measured the thermal indices itself [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]; the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days, and the Costa Rican units are high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. mitigation_mechanism: Measured cooling reaches crops: midday air temperature under Faidherbia albida canopies on Ethiopian wheat farms was up to 6°C lower than in the open field, poplar alley cropping in Germany was 3.4°C cooler than sole wheat on hot days, and lower heat load under Populus deltoides in India raised wheat grain yield by 6.8% [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6]. In the same Ethiopian study, a crop model found that the lower temperature under F. albida shade raised simulated wheat yield when nitrogen was applied, but without applied N simulated yield was extremely small and did not respond to temperature [ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. Tree shade lowers the temperature crops and animals experience: IPCC and other reviews state that agroforestry reduces ambient temperature and crop heat stress, with over-storey shade moderating severe temperature effects by 2–4°C and tree shading lowering air temperature by 4°C [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1]. A meta-analysis of field studies on Chinese farmland found summer air temperature 4.01% lower and relative humidity 13.45% higher in shelterbelt-protected than in unsheltered fields [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1].
caveats: Windbreak hedges in Senegal generally cause a slight temperature rise in the protected plots, with effects that vary by crop and growth stage [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. The Ethiopian, German, Indian, Senegalese and Chinese units come from rainfed cropping, and the German unit is high-income temperate evidence; the yield gain applies to hot conditions only [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_6, ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. Most units are reviews citing earlier studies and report cooling, a component of heat-stress impact [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1]. The shelterbelt cooling is a pooled meta-analysis result from upper-middle-income China, expressed as a modest percentage change in air temperature rather than a measured heat-stress loss [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. The Ethiopian cooling was measured on farm, but its yield link is modelled, and the model's null without applied N is among the no-benefit results in this row [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4].

mitigation_mechanism: Silvopastoral and pasture trees cut cattle heat stress: intensive shrub–tree–rotational pasture models in the dry Colombian Caribbean reduce it (Ocampo et al. 2012) [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1]. Tree shade in pastures is associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain (Abreu 2002) [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. In Nicaragua, Betancourt et al. 2003 found milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover, attributed to less heat stress and more foliage and fruit, and other studies found increases above 15% for cows grazing silvopasture compared with cows in full sun (Souza et al. 2000) [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2]. General reviews report the same cooling: over-storey shade moderates severe temperature (2–4°C) effects in silvopasture as well as crop systems, and tree shading can lower ambient temperature by 4°C [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_watts22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_vannoordwijk21_1].
caveats: Every unit reports a benefit, but none measures it in a heat event the authors call severe or extreme, and the transfer to LIC/LMIC rangelands is not direct: almost all the weight sits in upper-middle-income Brazil and Colombia, high-income Costa Rica and unlocated reviews, with Nicaragua the only lower-middle-income site [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1]. The Latin American silvopastoral units come from pastoral rangeland; the general reviews are applied here by default [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1]. caveats: Both units are second-hand readings in reviews (the biodrainage figure is from Ram et al. 2011), both from lower-middle-income India within the LIC/LMIC target, and neither reports a yield or livelihood outcome: they show water leaving the soil (evapotranspiration, a lower water table), not that crops or incomes recovered [ev_waterlogging_hazard_dobhal24_9, ev_waterlogging_hazard_singhlal18_1]. The 85 cm drop was measured under the strips themselves, against unvegetated fields; how far the effect reaches into the cropped inter-spaces is not stated [ev_waterlogging_hazard_singhlal18_1]. Neither says how big the effect on the hazard's impact is, so the strength is not quantified. mitigation_mechanism: Boundary and line plantings slow the wind: the zone of reduced wind speed typically extends 10 to 20 times tree height downwind (Tibke 1988), hedges protect sandy, poorly covered soils from wind erosion in Senegal, live fences serve as windbreaks in India, and a meta-analysis of field studies on Chinese farmland found wind speed 35.80% lower in shelterbelt-protected than in unsheltered fields [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15, ev_windbreak_protection_faosen24_12, ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4, ev_windbreak_protection_hao26_1]. The evidence about trees on farms in general points both ways: a review of smallholder agroforestry notes that trees on farm serve as windbreaks and shelterbelts and are used to rebuild property damaged during storms, while a Latin American adaptation review gives the planting of shade trees that damage existing infrastructure in storms as an example of increased vulnerability [ev_windbreak_protection_lasco14_1, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5]. In hurricane-hit coffee in Soconusco, Chiapas, vegetation management had significant effects on landslides but not on coffee harvest lost, with all farms reporting yield losses between 18 and 40% [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6].
caveats: Studies disagree across sub-practices, so the roll-up states conflicting evidence. The benefit side is the boundary and line plantings, which read as a moderate reduction: they slow everyday wind and wind erosion, entering as components rather than measured storm or cyclone losses [ev_windbreak_protection_dobhal24_15, ev_windbreak_protection_faosen24_12, ev_windbreak_protection_moran18_4, ev_windbreak_protection_hao26_1]. Against it, the shaded perennial-crop evidence shows no mitigation: after the Chiapas hurricane, coffee harvest loss did not differ with vegetation management, so shade trees did not protect the crop in that study [ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. The cross-cutting evidence is itself split between a smallholder review noting trees used as windbreaks and to rebuild storm-damaged property, and a Latin American adaptation review's example of shade trees that damage existing infrastructure in storms, the one harm finding in the row [ev_windbreak_protection_lasco14_1, ev_wind_cyclone_hazard_taboada20_5]. The separator is design and placement: a windbreak laid out to shelter a field is a different thing from shade trees over a crop or standing next to buildings when a storm hits, and no unit measures the effect in a storm the authors call severe or extreme, so the evidence does not say how far the windbreak benefit holds at storm or cyclone strength. Most units are reviews repeating earlier work. The Chinese shelterbelt result is from upper-middle-income China, and the Chiapas unit is crop-specific (coffee) from upper-middle-income Mexico, counted because shaded perennial-crop systems are judged on their host crop [ev_windbreak_protection_hao26_1, ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6].
